mcqs.question: Why can you always run SVD on a (500 x 20) ratings matrix, but you couldn't necessarily run standard eigen-decomposition on it directly?
options: SVD is just a renamed version of eigen-decomposition with no real difference
Eigen-decomposition requires a square matrix; SVD works on any m x n matrix by construction
SVD only works on matrices with more rows than columns
Eigen-decomposition is always faster, so SVD is only used when speed doesn't matter
mcqs.explanation: Eigen-decomposition (M = PDP⁻¹) is only defined for square matrices, and even then isn't guaranteed to exist. SVD is defined for any m x n matrix and always exists, because it's built from the eigen-decompositions of the always-square, always-symmetric AAᵀ and AᵀA. SVD works for either more rows or more columns.

mcqs.question: You truncate an SVD to the top 10 singular values out of 200. What guarantee does the Eckart-Young theorem give you about the result?
options: It guarantees zero reconstruction error as long as you keep at least one singular value
It guarantees the result will always be a valid probability distribution
It guarantees this truncated matrix is the best possible rank-10 approximation of the original, in a precise mathematical sense
It only applies when the original matrix is symmetric
mcqs.explanation: The Eckart-Young theorem states that truncating an SVD to the top k singular values gives the best possible rank-k approximation to the original matrix, minimizing reconstruction error among all rank-k matrices. It doesn't guarantee zero error (that only happens if the matrix already had rank ≤ k), and it applies to any matrix, not just symmetric ones.

mcqs.question: In the worked 3x2 example, keeping only the top singular-value term (sigma1=5) reconstructs column 1 exactly but drops column 2 entirely. Why does dropping a term lose an entire column rather than just shrinking every entry a little?
options: Because each singular value/vector pair in the sum contributes the structure for a specific direction in the data, and this particular matrix happens to have each column driven by a separate, non-overlapping direction
Because SVD always assigns exactly one singular value per column of the original matrix
Because this only happens when the matrix has more rows than columns
Dropping any singular value always destroys the same fraction of every column equally
mcqs.explanation: SVD writes A as a sum of rank-1 terms, each built from one singular value and its matching singular vectors; how that sum spreads across the original columns depends on the data's actual structure, not on a fixed one-value-per-column rule. In this specific example the two directions happen not to overlap across rows, so dropping one term zeroes out exactly the column it was responsible for — in a matrix without that clean separation, dropping a term would instead shrink many columns partially.

mcqs.question: If you kept both terms (sigma1 and sigma2) instead of truncating to rank-1 in the worked example, what would the reconstruction look like compared to the original A?
options: It would still lose information, since any SVD-based reconstruction is inherently lossy
It would require re-running SVD with a different algorithm to get an exact match
It would exactly reproduce the original matrix A, since keeping all singular values/vectors reconstructs the original matrix exactly with no approximation error
It would only approximate A more closely but never match it exactly, regardless of how many terms are kept
mcqs.explanation: SVD is an exact factorization, not inherently lossy — summing all of its rank-1 terms (all singular values and their vectors) reconstructs the original matrix A exactly. Approximation error is introduced specifically by truncating and dropping some of those terms; keeping every term is mathematically equivalent to not compressing at all.
